articles.headline: DEAD! His Life Work Ended, The Old Hero Dies.
articles.text:
DEAD!

HIS LIFE WORK ENDED, THE OLD HERO DIES.

Special Telegram to the BAD LANDS COW BOY.

MT. MCGREGOR, July 23.—General Grant died at eight o'clock. He passed quietly away, in the full possession of his senses and surrounded by his family. SPIZA.

We have only room to state, in addition to the above telegram, that General Grant had been failing for the last few days and it was manifest to all that his end was near. He had the determination to keep death at bay until his historical work was ended, when, there being nothing more to fight for, he, for the first time in his life surrendered. Future poets will sing his praises, future warriors will take him as a model, future painters will delight in picturing him as the third of that triumvirate, dear to every American's heart, Washington-Lincoln-Grant.
articles.summary: Special telegram to the Cow Boy announcing the death of General U. S. Grant at Mt. McGregor that morning, with a short tribute.

articles.text: Secretary Lamar has put his foot into it in bad shape in ordering the opening of the Texas trails. He puts his own power against the wishes of every state and territory on the line of the trail, besides that of every stock organization between here and Texas. Beyond that, he overrules laws made by the states and territories crossed by the Texas trail against this very invasion. More than all this, he takes the word of the few men driving cattle from Texas that the cattle are not infectious, against the combined statements of all others that they either are or are probably so. At present the trail advocates are decidedly on top.
articles.summary: Editorial criticizing Interior Secretary Lamar for ordering the Texas cattle trails opened despite state and territorial quarantine laws.

articles.text: At last visitors to Niagara Falls can be free from the extortionate charges that have coupled the name of that grandest work of nature with all manner of greed. The American side of the river near the Falls, Goat island and the small islands north and south of it, including Bath island have all been bought by the state of New York and the whole is now turned into a free public park. This movement is one that will go far toward redeeming New York from the load of shame that oppresses her legislation. New York virtually makes a national gift to the United States of Niagara Falls and should receive every credit therefor.
articles.summary: Editorial praising New York's purchase of the American side of Niagara Falls as a free public park.

articles.text: Great excitement has recently been caused in the east and especially in Chicago, from several cases of poisoning from dried beef said to come from the Chicago stock yards. At Momence, Ill., there were thirty-four cases and other isolated cases are being reported from other places. The poison is probably germinated from putrefaction and its action is very severe. The Chicago packers are unanimously of the opinion that the beef came from an irresponsible dealer and desire the strictest investigation and the blame laid to the proper source. In Adrian, Mich., a case has been reported where the poisoning came from canned beef, but in most instances it comes from dried beef.
articles.summary: Note on dried-beef poisoning cases in Illinois and Michigan traced to Chicago.

articles.text: John Roach, America's greatest shipbuilder, has been forced into bankruptcy by Secretaries Whitney and Garland. On the shallowest of pretences, they have refused to accept the Dolphin, a vessel built by Roach under government contract and under the personal supervision of a committee appointed by the government. Aside from the Dolphin, Roach had contracts for several other vessels which Attorney General Garland now declares illegal. The whole matter is a scheme on the part of Whitney and Garland, backed by enemies of Roach to ruin the latter. At present it looks like a success, but the law may step in and prove that it is mightier than Attorney General Garland.
articles.summary: Editorial blaming Secretaries Whitney and Garland for shipbuilder John Roach's bankruptcy over the Dolphin.

articles.text: The Mormons have begun showing their hand in such a way that it is impossible for the government longer to avoid taking cognizance of their actions. The laws passed respecting their marriage customs have no effect whatever and in other respects they are living in direct violation to the law. Their crowning act of treason was on the 4th. of July, when all national flags on public buildings were lowered to half-mast. This is an insult to our flag that no nation on the face of the earth dare put upon the United States. That such "scum de la scum" as the Mormons should not only live in open defiance of the law, but should go out of their way to insult the flag can not be endured. It calls for instant and condign punishment that a Republican administration would not be long in inflicting. Add to all this the fact that even now troops are being brought into Salt Lake City to quell a threatened disturbance on the Mormon's national holiday and we have a state of affairs only explained by the liberty of our institutions. This liberty has been trampled on and villified long enough. It is time for the government to take a hand and crush forever such a disgrace as Mormonism.
articles.summary: Editorial attacking the Mormons over the half-masted flags of July 4 in Salt Lake City and calling for federal punishment.

articles.text: Joseph Nimmo, Jr., chief of the bureau of statistics and author of the recent "Report in regard to the Range and Ranch cattle business of the United States" is already collecting the material for a popular work on the subject. The government edition of his work is exhausted and the call for it has been so large that it shows a good opening for the work Mr. Nimmo has in contemplation. It is a field entirely unoccupied except by newspapers and we wish the author every success in his undertaking. Mr. Nimmo informs us that he intends soon making a tour of inspection of the range country and will spend some time in the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: Joseph Nimmo, Jr., plans a popular book on the range cattle business and a tour of the range country including the Bad Lands.

articles.text: According to the latest reports there are very nearly, if not quite 50,000,000 cattle in the United States. Of these Texas stands at the head of the list with 9,000,000. Iowa comes next with over 3,500,000. Then comes Missouri, New York, Illinois and Kansas in the order named with over 2,000,000 each. Ohio, Nebraska, Pennsylvania, Indiana, Wisconsin, Wyoming and Indian Territory, following with numbers from a few over a million in the latter to nearly two million in the former. Montana has nearly 800,000 and Dakota has nearly 400,000. Little Rhody foots the list with 35,000.
articles.summary: Statistics on U.S. cattle numbers by state and territory.

articles.text: The cattle raisers of Dakota have an advantage over those of Wyoming which is scarcely valued as it should be. This is in the matter of freight rates. Whatever can be said in reference to rates charged by the Northern Pacific in other matters, it must be acknowledged that their rates on cattle are extremely low. In car-load lots, according to Nimmo's report, the tariff is at the rate of fifty-three cents a hundred miles from Chicago to New York, the rate on the Union Pecific is sixty cents and that on the Northern Pacific is fifty-six cents. When we notice that there are many roads competing for the business from Chicago to New York and that there is no competition on the Northern Pacific, it is manifest that the latter is giving every encouragement to cattle raising. In Dakota especially, as we started to remark, do these rates benefit our cowmen. The average rate per head from Dakota shipping points to Chicago is $4.88. The rate from Wyoming points is $7.22. Thus the Dakota cattleman gains an additional profit of $2.34 per head over his Wyoming brother. In dealing with large herds this is a very neat figure to save.
articles.summary: Editorial note that Northern Pacific cattle freight rates give Dakota cattlemen a $2.34-per-head advantage over Wyoming.

articles.text: Dr. H. M. Jorgens and family start this afternoon for Cave Hills. Messrs. Powers and Johnson, of Grand Rapids, Mich., came last night and start with E. G. Paddock, on their way to Spearfish. On his return trip, Mr. Paddock will bring back Mrs. Fred Willard.

articles.text: A very pleasant social gathering took place at the Rowe, Parker & Easton cattle ranch, on the evening of the 12th of July. Music, singing and dancing were all on the evening's programme. At twelve o'clock supper was served. It was voted by all in attendance to be the most pleasant evening ever spent by the young people of the Little Beaver.
articles.summary: A social evening was held July 12 at the Rowe, Parker & Easton ranch on the Little Beaver.

articles.text: The Chimney Butte ranch was the place and Merrifield and Ferris Bros. were the hosts, that entertained a party last Saturday in a way to warm one's heart to Bad Lands hospitality. Riding, horse-racing, shooting, a runaway and a good exhibition of bucking, crowned by a bountiful ranch supper, completed an afternoon of pleasure long to be remembered by the participants.
articles.summary: Merrifield and the Ferris brothers hosted a party with riding, racing, shooting and bucking at the Chimney Butte ranch on Saturday.

articles.text: Grasshoppers or seventeen-year locusts, authorities differ, are doing great damage in Montana and north-western Dakota. Many fields of grain north of the Yellowstone, in Montana and some of the ranges south of the Yellowstone have been nearly or quite destroyed. It is doubtful if they will get as far south as the railroad in time to do much damage. Their advance is slow and they are now at least seventy-five miles from the end of the wheat belt, which ends at Belfield. We advise our eastern neighbors to harvest their grain as soon as possible.
articles.summary: Grasshoppers or locusts are damaging grain and ranges in Montana and northwestern Dakota.

articles.headline: In Justice Gordon's Court.
articles.text:
In Justice Gordon's Court.

Territory vs R. Roberts. } Assault.

At the regular session of Justice Gordon's court yesterday afternoon, the only case on the docket was the assault case against Robert Roberts. Nate. Baker, a gentleman of elegant leisure, who rode into town on a tie and brake-beam pass, was the complaining witness.

Court was opened at three o'clock by sheriff Lincoln Lee. The first witness was the plaintiff, Mr. Nathaniel Baker. He testified that his home was the same as that of his satanic majesty and that he was a hunter, having spent all his life killing time. Occasionally, or about seven times a day, he branched into a profession he had down finer than a bug's bill, that of "bumming chuck." As a means of livelihood, outside of his business and profession, he was a scissors-grinder. To prove his statement he drew the implements of his trade from his vest pocket; a piece of scoria for a grindstone and a broken-bladed penknife for a screw-driver. He further stated that entering the doxology works of the prisoner at the bar he had been saluted by the discharge of a deadly weapon, aimed in his direction and held in the hands of the aforesaid prisoner. That he had then sworn out a complaint before Justice Gordon and had the prisoner arrested. On cross-examination he testified that his home was in Belfield. The court then very properly over-ruled the motion of defendant's counsel to quash the case, owing to the conflicting evidence concerning the plaintiff's residence by complaining witness, holding that there was no conflict in his statements.

Fred Willard was then sworn. He testified that he was a barber by trade and very nervous by temperament. That he had been extremely bothered in the practice of his tonsorial occupation by defendant playfully holding him up whenever he had a splinter or two. The prosecuting witness had come into his place of business, complaining that the defendant had held him up for a coin about as big as a dollar or a dollar and a half or two dollars. As witness had often suffered in the same way he willingly loaned the prosecuting witness a six-shooter and took pains to look carefully at the loads and see that the powder and ball were removed from the cartridges. The complaining witness then started for Mr. Roberts place of business and the next witness saw was the form of Mr. Baker fairly clawing the air in a race against time and bullets. He also remembered that Mr. Baker while jumping over a ten-foot corral fence casually remarked something about murder and things. He also saw Mr. Roberts in hot pursuit who playfully kept up his target practice at a variegated piece of cloth on the sag of Mr. Baker's pants, commenting meanwhile to the effect that, "Nobody but a rank tenderfoot would turn loose on him."

During the course of the trial the testimony had been several times interrupted by the defendant and it was found necessary to handcuff and gag him and then lay him in a corner where the court feather-weights Shorty and Sam Whitney placidly anchored him down by sitting on him.

Being released, the defendant testified that his name was Robert Roberts. That his home was in Landdasant Anglesay Bightyoughertougueough, Great Britain. That he was a foreign missionary sent out by his home congregation to spread the glad tidings of great joy among the buttes and coolies of the Bad Lands. Here the prisoner had a convulsion of the countenance which the court interpreter declared to be a wink. On suspicion, and because the boys were getting dry, the court immediately found the prisoner guilty of breach of promise, ordered the prosecuting witness to resume his tie pass and adjourned court to try and induce a little boy to buy a winter suit that would have looked baggy on Myers, the Fat.
articles.summary: Burlesque report of Justice Gordon's court trying Robert Roberts for firing on tramp Nate Baker; Roberts was found 'guilty of breach of promise' and Baker sent on his way.
